title: Inside Nvidia’s Plan to Accelerate Quantum Error Correction - HPCwire
html:
One of the biggest hurdles to building useful quantum computers is fixing the errors that inevitably arise in quantum processing. As part of the quantum computing co-design platform that Nvidia, IBM, and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory unveiled at SC26 last week is a plan to build powerful error decoders using real-time AI powered by GPUs.

Error rates in quantum computing are caused by a range of conditions, including environmental noise, qubit decoherence, imperfect controls, and other causes of bit-flips and phase-flip errors. The rate of raw physical errors is typically around 0.1% to 1% in quantum computing, which is orders of magnitude higher than for classical computing.

QC builders use a range of techniques to address quantum errors. There are error suppression techniques, such as dynamical decoupling and gate and pulse shaping, as well as error mitigation routines, such as zero-noise extrapolation and probabilistic error cancellation. However, to build large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers, it’s generally accepted that real-time quantum error correction (QEC) is needed.

QEC combines several techniques. For starters, a collection of physical qubits are grouped together to create a single logical qubit, reducing the odds that a single error in any one physical qubits is propagated to the remainder of the enabled qubits. QEC also involves classical computing “decoders” that analyze the data flowing off of stabilizer checks and applying the necessary correction in real time.

NVQLink

According to Sam Stanwyck, director of quantum product at Nvidia, there has been real progress made in building decoders over the past couple of years.

“When we first started working in quantum computing, you couldn’t use a quantum computer at all. They were they were toys,” Stanwyck said. “And what people needed were the most powerful simulators possible of quantum computers just to understand what they might run on them to start developing algorithms and applications, to start designing the future systems.”

For the past two years, the focus has shifted to enabling logical qubits and building QEC systems, along with better decoders.

“The reason quantum computing can work at all is because we can come up with the capability to decode errors in real-time faster than they’re being made,” Stanwyck told HPCwire at SC26. “We built NVQLink as an open reference architecture to provide developers with the low latency interconnect to even develop these decoders.”

The quantum computing co-design platform that Nvidia, IBM, and Fermilab have in mind will enable developers to innovate at multiple layers, including the decoding layer, the logical architectural layer, as well as the algorithm and application layer.

As part of the collaboration unveiled last week, an Nvidia DGX B200 system will be co-located with an IBM Quantum Nighthawk computer to provide real-time QEC. Nighthawk is IBM’s most powerful superconducting, gate-based quantum computer. The current Nighthawk r2 system features 120 programmable qubits and is capable of running up to 7,500 two-qubit operations. Announced earlier this month, the Nighthawk r3 system will be capable of executing 10,000 quantum operations across 520 qubits, double that with two systems connected.

Renders of IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3 (L), and IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 (R), IBM’s most powerful processors designed to support 10,000 quantum operations in 2027 (Credit: IBM)

The collaboration also involves Fermilab and its Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems (SQMS) Center. The partners will work to see how they can sample data from quantum interactions running across multiple quantum processors and inject corrections as needed. They will also explore how QC can enable the execution of complex calculations in high-energy and nuclear physics that are beyond the reach of classical systems alone, such as such as lattice gauge theories, neutrino interactions and nuclear simulations.

Correcting quantum errors will be instrumental in building quantum processing units (QPUs) that can augment classical supercomputers. Currently, QEC can be done within about 300 milliseconds of microseconds of processing, said Ian Buck, the vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia.

“We want to get down to 10 in order to do real time error correction and to keep the calculation going, to inject corrections into the computation in real time to maintain a one long continuous processing on a quantum computer,” he said during his SC26 presentation last week.

Improving QEC will be an area of constant focus for QC builders. As Stanwyck noted, we still don’t know what the best decoder is going to be, and the current approaches may be replaced with something better. With that said, the new CUDA-Q decoders that Nvidia is building should provide a big boost in QEC productivity.

“Previously, you run a quantum computation, you’d get a whole bunch of data. It would take literally 12 weeks of data processing to see if your algorithm or your approach improves things,” Buck said. “Using the new CUDA-Q decoder, a technique called trajectory calibrated belief calibration and beam search, that 12 weeks just went down to about 45 minutes on a GPU with CUDA.”
